clue.text: Getting rid of bribes flung back in face

indicators.note: in places the turned bribes inside the word for face

parts.note: dial is slang for a face, as well as a clock face

indicators.note: flung back says the word bribes is thrown into reverse order

parts.note: a sop is a small bribe to keep someone quiet

explanation.surface: Someone throwing bribes back in the briber's face to be rid of them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Face' looks like the target of the throw, but it is the outer word, slang for a face.
explanation.definitionFit: Disposal is the act of discarding something, matching a noun-like gerund for removal.

clue.text: Swindle mum, making money

parts.note: to do someone is slang for to cheat them
mum means silent, and sh is a call for silence

explanation.surface: Someone defrauding their mother to earn cash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mum' looks like a mother, but it means keeping quiet.
explanation.definitionFit: Dosh is British slang for cash.

clue.text: Want to have bishop's authority over king

parts.note: a see is the area under a bishop's authority
K is king in chess notation

explanation.surface: A church leader wanting power over the monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over' places SEE above K in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: To seek something is to look for it or try to obtain it, much as to want it.

clue.text: Defeat ended game

parts.note: something over is finished
a match is a game

explanation.surface: A finished game that ended in a loss.
explanation.definitionFit: To overmatch an opponent is to be too strong for them and so beat them.

clue.text: One with an end in sight?

definitions.text: One with an end in sight?

parts.words: One with an end in sight?
parts.note: surface reading: someone whose goal is nearly reached
setter's reading: one whose aim is to put an end to something, here slavery

explanation.surface: Someone close to finishing a long task.
explanation.walkthrough: 'End in sight' usually means nearly done; here the end is the one the person campaigns for.
explanation.definitionFit: Historically these campaigners sought to stop slavery, with its termination as their whole goal.

clue.text: Doctrinaire person gets chap in a temper

indicators.note: in puts the chap's name inside the word for a temper

parts.note: a pet is a fit of sulky temper
Dan is any man's name, so a chap

explanation.surface: A rigid, opinionated person flies into a rage when a man arrives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Temper' suggests anger; a pet is a sulky fit, a sense many solvers miss.
explanation.definitionFit: A pedant insists rigidly on rules and formal correctness, a fair description of a doctrinaire type.

clue.text: Out in Lake Victoria

indicators.note: in says the letters sit inside the run of the following words

parts.note: letters running across the two words

explanation.surface: Something out on the waters of Africa's great lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out' is a verb here, as in to out someone from a house.
explanation.definitionFit: To out a tenant, in the verb sense, is to throw them out of a property.

clue.text: Unconventional art coach, I'm not using colours

indicators.note: unconventional means not in the usual order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the fodder letters

explanation.surface: An offbeat art teacher announcing they paint without colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Achromatic means without hue, made only of black, white and greys.

clue.text: Old Times composer, perhaps, a model to one like me?

parts.note: a type is a model or standard example
the clue speaks as the crossword's setter

explanation.surface: The setter musing that an old Times worker might be their role model.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Composer' suggests music, but in printing a compositor sets type. 'Perhaps' flags an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Before computers, a newspaper's compositor assembled metal type into pages, so a typesetter is an example.

clue.text: Poet penning English sketch in outline

indicators.note: a poet penning something holds it within, so the poet's name wraps the letter

parts.note: John Skelton was a Tudor poet
E is the standard abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A poet writing an English piece, drafting it first in rough outline.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sketch' looks like part of the writing scene, but 'sketch in outline' is the definition, a verb phrase. E sits inside SKELTON.
explanation.definitionFit: To skeleton a plan, used as a verb, is to draft its bare framework, just as a rough sketch does.

clue.text: Incomplete description after motorway accident

indicators.note: incomplete means the word for description loses its final letter
after sends the description piece second, behind the motorway letters

parts.note: the M1 is Britain's main north-south motorway, written MI
the shape of something is a description of its form

explanation.surface: A sketchy witness report given after a crash on the motorway.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is a British motorway; its digit 1 stands in for the letter I. SHAPE drops its E.
explanation.definitionFit: A mishap is an unlucky accident, usually minor, so the two words are synonyms.

clue.text: Stewed pear — yet in tin can

indicators.note: stewed fruit is cooked down and mixed up, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: the fodder letters

explanation.surface: A recipe note: stewed pear, yet tinned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can' looks like the tin from the kitchen, but it is US slang for prison.
explanation.definitionFit: Can is American slang for jail, and a penitentiary is a US state or federal prison.

clue.text: Having no first-hand experience?

parts.note: surface reading: never having experienced something personally
setter's reading: no hand comes first, as both hands are equally skilled

explanation.surface: Someone who knows things only second-hand, never from direct experience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First-hand' is an idiom for direct; read literally, it means a leading or dominant hand.
explanation.definitionFit: An ambidextrous person uses left and right equally well, so neither one is their first or preferred.

clue.text: Evil, bad pieces fabricated about Liberal

indicators.note: about means going round, so the jumble wraps the party letter
fabricated means made up, so these letters are built into new order

parts.note: the fodder letters
L is the standard abbreviation for Liberal

explanation.surface: Smears made up about a Liberal politician are vile.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bad' looks like an anagram signal, but it is part of the fodder; the signal is 'fabricated'.
explanation.definitionFit: Despicable means deserving contempt, wicked, so it serves as an adjective for evil.

clue.text: A nominal inheritance

parts.note: surface reading: a legacy so tiny it is barely worth anything
setter's reading: relating to a name, so a name passed down from a father

explanation.surface: A token bequest left in someone's will.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nominal' usually means token; here it means of a name.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a surname derived from one's father or ancestor, such as Johnson, son of John.

clue.text: Name on end of title deed to make legal

indicators.note: end of picks only the last letter of the word title

parts.note: the last letter of title
N is a standard abbreviation for name
an act is a deed

explanation.surface: Adding a name to a title deed so that it becomes legally binding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Name on' places N after E in the across entry.
explanation.definitionFit: To enact a bill is to pass it into law, which makes it legal.

clue.text: I can get queen ant on the move

parts.note: taken as written
a tin is a can
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the queen's cipher
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone boasting they can keep a queen ant moving about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can' looks like a verb here, but it is a noun: a tin.
explanation.definitionFit: Itinerant describes someone who travels from place to place, never settling.

clue.text: OPEC soon compromise, initially dropping 50% throughout to make savings

indicators.note: each word in turn loses its first half, the opening letters being dropped

parts.note: taken as written; its last half is kept
taken as written; its last half is kept
taken as written; its last half is kept

explanation.surface: Oil producers agreeing to cut output by half to save money.
explanation.walkthrough: OPEC loses OP, SOON loses SO, COMPROMISE loses COMPR. OPEC is the oil producers' cartel.
explanation.definitionFit: To economise is to spend less and cut costs, which makes savings.

clue.text: Fish caught in Scottish one, maybe

parts.note: a perch is a freshwater fish

indicators.note: something caught in a thing is trapped inside it, so the cricket letter goes within

parts.note: ane is the Scots form of one
c. means caught on a cricket scoresheet

explanation.surface: A fisherman wondering whether a fish was landed in Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caught' looks like the fishing verb, but it is the cricket abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Perchance is an old-fashioned word for perhaps, meaning possibly or by chance.

clue.text: Fruit that is old and turning bad

parts.note: O is the standard abbreviation for old

indicators.note: turning means the word for bad is read the other way round

parts.note: evil means wicked, bad

explanation.surface: A piece of fruit past its best and starting to go off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turning bad' reads as rotting fruit, but turning is the reversal signal and bad is a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: The olive is the small oily stone fruit of the Mediterranean olive tree.

clue.text: Talking of a time during change-over

indicators.note: during places the time phrase inside the change-over word

parts.note: a conversion is a change from one thing to another
a is taken as written and T abbreviates time

explanation.surface: Someone chatting about an era during a period of transition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Talking' is used as a noun, as in 'talking is not allowed'.
explanation.definitionFit: Conversation is spoken exchange between people, so talking in the noun sense.

clue.text: Rub out Times puzzle finally

parts.note: eras are times or ages

indicators.note: finally takes only the closing letter of the word puzzle

parts.note: the last letter of puzzle

explanation.surface: Wiping clean the Times crossword at last.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Times' looks like the newspaper, but it is a plain plural.
explanation.definitionFit: To erase writing is to remove it by rubbing, so a direct synonym for rub out.

clue.text: State area covered by island

indicators.note: in a down entry, being covered by something means sitting beneath it, so the area letter comes second

parts.note: IOW is the Isle of Wight, off England's south coast
A is the abbreviation for area

explanation.surface: A region of land lying under an island.
explanation.walkthrough: IOW is the Isle of Wight, a common crossword island.
explanation.definitionFit: This is one of the fifty United States, a farming region in the Midwest, so a fair example of a state.

clue.text: Decorate supporter of crew

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to adorn, as in to array with garlands
second meaning: the floor of a ship, which bears up the sailors

explanation.surface: Honouring someone who backs a team of rowers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supporter' suggests a fan; here it is what physically holds the crew up.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to adorn, and the noun is the ship's floor on which sailors stand.

clue.text: Lament bird that's extinct in Scots upland

indicators.note: in places the extinct bird inside the upland word

parts.note: a ben is a Scottish mountain, as in Ben Nevis
the moa was a giant flightless New Zealand bird, now extinct

explanation.surface: Mourning the loss of a bird species from the Scottish hills.
explanation.definitionFit: To bemoan is to express grief or regret over something, the same as to lament it.

clue.text: He sings but one musical sound

parts.note: bar can mean except, as in 'all bar one'
I is the Roman numeral one
a tone is a musical sound

explanation.surface: A singer who produces only a single musical note.
explanation.walkthrough: 'But one' reads as 'only one', yet but is BAR (except) and one is I.
explanation.definitionFit: A baritone is a male singer whose voice lies between tenor and bass, so a man who sings.

clue.text: Avoid being sweet with opponents at bridge

parts.note: East and South are opposing partnerships at bridge
a chew is a chewy sweet or candy

explanation.surface: A bridge player trying not to look sugary toward rival players.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' lets the bridge pair sit alongside the sweet. At bridge the players are North, South, East and West; E and S are on opposite sides.
explanation.definitionFit: To eschew something is to deliberately abstain from or shun it.

clue.text: Doctor's replacement joining explorer in London area

indicators.note: joining says the two pieces are attached one after the other

parts.note: Mr Hyde takes the place of Dr Jekyll in Stevenson's story
Mungo Park was a Scottish explorer of the Niger

explanation.surface: A locum doctor teaming up with an adventurer somewhere in the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: The doctor is Jekyll, whose other self Hyde replaces him.
explanation.definitionFit: Hyde Park is the large royal park in central London.
